why_this_tool: Amazon SageMaker documents the full monitoring loop in one place (capture, baseline, scheduled checks, violations, metrics and alarms), and its availability-change page maps each part to open-source replacements you can run on a laptop.
alternatives: Evidently is an open-source library that computes quality and drift reports anywhere Python runs; whylogs logs compact statistical profiles for later comparison; Great Expectations validates data against declared expectations but does not measure drift statistically; Prometheus with Alertmanager and Grafana handles metric storage, alert routing and dashboards but needs you to compute the model metrics yourself; Amazon CloudWatch is the managed metric and alarm service that SageMaker monitoring emits into.

steps.why: Data quality monitoring means nothing without a baseline to compare against. The constraints are the contract every later batch is checked against.

steps.do: Compare a corrupted serving batch (missing values, a changed type, an out-of-range column) against the baseline and write the result in the documented violations layout.

steps.why: The kinds of drift are measured differently and call for different responses. Sorting real findings into the four types fixes the vocabulary.

steps.do: Configure data capture for your model: a real endpoint needs a paid cloud account, so on the laptop wrap a local prediction function to append each request and response to a dated file with a unique inference id.
steps.done_when: After twenty local predictions the capture file holds twenty records, each with input, output, timestamp and inference id.
steps.why: Monitoring can only analyse what was recorded. The inference id is what later makes it possible to attach ground truth to a prediction.

steps.do: Write delayed ground truth labels keyed by inference id, join them to the captured predictions and compute model quality metrics against a baseline of the same metrics.
steps.done_when: A merged table shows prediction and label side by side, and a metric such as accuracy is printed for the baseline and the current window.
steps.why: Accuracy can only be monitored once labels arrive, often days later. The join is where most model quality pipelines break.

steps.do: Configure an alerting rule on one drift metric and one quality metric with a threshold and an evaluation period. CloudWatch alarms need a cloud account, so on the laptop emit the metrics to a local file and have a script exit with a failure when the threshold is breached.
steps.done_when: The clean batch passes the rule and the shifted batch makes the script fail with a message naming the metric and threshold.
steps.why: A dashboard nobody watches does not protect a model. The rule turns a metric into a page or a retraining trigger.

steps.do: Query the results of your last runs the way the documentation lists executions and opens the violations report, then write a short response runbook: who is paged, what is checked first, and when retraining is triggered.
steps.done_when: Your runbook maps each violation type from your report to a named first action and an escalation rule.
steps.why: Alerting is only half the job; the response has to be decided before the alert fires. Reading the violations report is the first action in any such runbook.

steps.do: Reproduce the whole check as a scheduled job: baseline files from version control, the pinned environment, the latest capture window in, a report and an exit status out. A managed monitoring schedule needs a cloud account, so use a local scheduler or a continuous integration job on a fixed interval.
steps.done_when: Two consecutive scheduled runs produce two dated reports with no manual action.

steps.why: Monitoring that runs only when someone remembers is not monitoring. Scheduling on a fixed window is also what makes results comparable between runs.

steps.do: Run a segment-sliced bias check and a feature attribution comparison on the captured data. The managed bias and explainability monitors need a paid cloud account, so compute per-segment metrics and feature importance rankings locally against the baseline.
steps.done_when: You have one per-segment metric table and one ranked feature importance list, each for baseline and current data, with differences flagged.

steps.why: A model can keep its overall accuracy while degrading for one group or relying on different features. These two monitors catch what data and quality checks miss.

steps.done_when: A drifting traffic window produces a violations report and a fired alert without manual steps, and a clean window produces neither.
